difficultyReason: The stimulus presents tension between two sets of data — antibiotic resistance rates rising while prescriptions fall — requiring the student to identify the hedged inference that correctly resolves the tension without overclaiming causation or direction. Traps include an opposite-direction answer and a too-strong absolute claim.
stimulus: A longitudinal study tracked antibiotic prescription rates and antibiotic-resistant infection rates across seventeen hospitals over a twelve-year period. In hospitals where prescription rates declined by more than 20 percent, antibiotic-resistant infection rates nonetheless increased during the first five years of the study. After the fifth year, however, those same hospitals began showing smaller increases in resistance rates than hospitals where prescription rates had remained stable or risen. Hospitals that had never reduced prescription rates showed the steepest and most consistent increases in resistance rates over the full twelve years.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reducing antibiotic prescriptions eliminates the development of antibiotic-resistant infections within five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibiotic-resistant infections are more dangerous in hospitals that never reduced prescription rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reducing antibiotic prescription rates may slow the growth of antibiotic resistance over time, even if resistance continues to increase initially.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antibiotic resistance rates are determined primarily by prescription practices within individual hospitals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hospitals that reduced prescriptions the most aggressively will eventually see antibiotic resistance rates decline to zero.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that hospitals with reduced prescriptions still saw rising resistance early on but smaller increases later compared to non-reducing hospitals. This hedged pattern — continued increase, but at a slower rate — directly supports the inference that reduction may slow resistance growth over time without eliminating it. 'May' and 'even if' correctly hedge against the early-period anomaly.
explanations.A: Too strong: the stimulus shows resistance still increased in the first five years in reducing hospitals; it was never eliminated.
explanations.B: Scope creep and unsupported: the stimulus measures resistance rates, not danger or severity of individual infections. No comparison of danger is offered.
explanations.D: Too strong: 'determined primarily' is an absolute causal claim the stimulus does not support; many other factors could influence resistance rates.
explanations.E: Too strong and opposite extrapolation: the stimulus shows resistance continued rising even in reducing hospitals; projecting it to 'zero' inverts and overclaims the trend.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves an economic subgroup exception (small manufacturers diverging from the broader manufacturing trend) requiring the student to pick the inference that correctly scopes the claim to that subgroup without generalizing or inverting the finding. Trap answers generalize to all manufacturers or assign an incorrect causal direction.
stimulus: Data from a national trade association survey show that overall manufacturing output declined by 8 percent last year, yet manufacturers with fewer than fifty employees reported a 3 percent increase in output over the same period. The survey also found that small manufacturers — those with fewer than fifty employees — were nearly twice as likely as large manufacturers to have introduced a new product line within the preceding eighteen months. Large manufacturers, by contrast, concentrated resources on streamlining existing production processes.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Introducing new product lines is the primary driver of output growth for all manufacturing firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Large manufacturers will eventually adopt the same strategies used by small manufacturers in order to reverse their output declines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some manufacturers were able to increase output during a period of general manufacturing decline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Streamlining existing production processes consistently reduces manufacturing output.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small manufacturers outperform large manufacturers across all major economic indicators.

explanations.correct: The survey explicitly states that small manufacturers (fewer than 50 employees) saw a 3 percent output increase during a period when overall manufacturing output fell 8 percent. Therefore, at least some manufacturers (specifically small ones) increased output during general decline — a direct, hedged inference from the data.
explanations.A: Too strong and scope creep: 'primary driver for all manufacturing firms' is not established; the stimulus only reports a correlation for small manufacturers, and no causal primacy is stated.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus makes no predictions about future strategy adoption by large manufacturers.
explanations.D: Opposite direction / too strong: the stimulus says large manufacturers focused on streamlining, but does not establish that streamlining caused their decline or that it consistently reduces output.
explanations.E: Scope creep and too strong: the stimulus addresses only output; 'all major economic indicators' vastly overgeneralizes.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves environmental data with a counterintuitive directional twist: a species thrives in degraded habitat under certain conditions but not others. The correct answer requires tracking two interacting variables. Traps include an opposite-direction answer and one that confuses necessary vs. sufficient conditions.
stimulus: Field surveys in a coastal wetland region found that populations of the spotted marsh wren were larger in moderately degraded wetlands — those affected by agricultural runoff but retaining native vegetation — than in pristine wetlands with no runoff exposure. However, in severely degraded wetlands where native vegetation had been replaced by invasive species, spotted marsh wren populations were nearly absent. Ornithologists noted that moderately degraded wetlands tended to have elevated insect populations, a primary food source for the wren, while pristine wetlands had insect populations of average density.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agricultural runoff benefits all wetland bird species by increasing insect populations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The spotted marsh wren thrives in any wetland environment that has been exposed to agricultural runoff.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Native vegetation is more important to spotted marsh wren population size than insect abundance alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of native vegetation may be a necessary condition for agricultural runoff to support spotted marsh wren populations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wetland degradation is, on balance, beneficial to the spotted marsh wren's long-term survival as a species.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that runoff + native vegetation → larger wren populations, but runoff + no native vegetation (severe degradation) → nearly absent populations. This pattern supports the inference that native vegetation may be a necessary condition for runoff to benefit wrens — without it, runoff alone does not support the population. 'May be' appropriately hedges the causal claim.
explanations.A: Too strong and scope creep: the stimulus addresses only the spotted marsh wren, not all wetland bird species, and does not establish a universal benefit.
explanations.B: Too strong: the severely degraded wetlands also had runoff exposure, yet wren populations were nearly absent — directly contradicting this claim.
explanations.C: This inverts or misweights the data: the stimulus suggests insect abundance (elevated in moderately degraded wetlands) does help wrens, but the critical variable distinguishing the two degraded wetland types is native vegetation. The answer form ('more important than insect abundance alone') isn't cleanly supported because insect abundance and vegetation are confounded in the data; D is the more precise and better-supported inference.
explanations.E: Too strong and opposite direction: severe degradation nearly eliminates wren populations; calling degradation 'on balance beneficial' to the species' long-term survival is not supported.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves a policy evaluation with a counterintuitive finding: a mandatory disclosure law reduced the targeted behavior in large firms but increased it in small firms. The correct answer must be scoped precisely to one subgroup. Traps include answers that generalize across firm size or that assign causation the stimulus does not establish.
stimulus: A state legislature passed a law requiring all businesses to disclose the wages paid to employees in each job category. An independent evaluation conducted two years after implementation found that the gender wage gap — the difference between average pay for men and women in equivalent positions — narrowed significantly at firms with more than 500 employees. At firms with fewer than 100 employees, however, the gender wage gap widened slightly in the two years following the law's implementation, a change the evaluators attributed to increased male retention bonuses at those firms rather than to reduced female wages.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mandatory wage disclosure laws reliably narrow the gender wage gap across all firm sizes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The wage disclosure law failed to achieve its intended effect and should be repealed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gender wage gap narrowed at large firms following the implementation of the wage disclosure law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Small firms deliberately used retention bonuses to circumvent the intent of the wage disclosure law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mandatory wage disclosure is more effective than any other policy intervention at closing the gender wage gap.

explanations.correct: The evaluation directly states that the gender wage gap narrowed significantly at firms with more than 500 employees in the two years after the law. This is a straightforward factual inference from the stimulus, precisely scoped to large firms.
explanations.A: Too strong: the stimulus shows the gap did not narrow — indeed widened — at small firms, directly contradicting universal applicability across all firm sizes.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus doesn't identify the law's 'intended effect' or make a normative recommendation about repeal. The law had mixed effects; calling it a failure and recommending repeal goes beyond the data.
explanations.D: Too strong / unsupported intent: the evaluators attribute the gap widening to increased male retention bonuses, but 'deliberately circumvent' imputes motive that the stimulus does not establish.
explanations.E: Scope creep and too strong: no comparison to other policy interventions is made in the stimulus.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents historical data about a technology adoption pattern with a counterintuitive finding: early adopters fared worse than late adopters in one dimension. The correct inference must track the specific dimension without overgeneralizing. Multiple plausible but unsupported answers are available.
stimulus: Historical records from the early railroad era in North America indicate that the first companies to build steam-powered rail lines in a given region frequently went bankrupt within fifteen years, while companies that entered the same regional markets ten to twenty years later tended to remain solvent for significantly longer periods. Engineers of the later period benefited from design improvements developed by earlier firms, and the later companies' rail lines required substantially less maintenance expenditure per mile than those of pioneer firms. Passenger volumes on both early and late lines were comparable during their respective first decades of operation.
questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early railroad companies in North America were poorly managed compared to later entrants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Being the first to enter a regional railroad market was, in at least some cases, a financial disadvantage rather than an advantage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Technological innovation in rail engineering was the sole cause of the financial failures among pioneer railroad companies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passenger demand for rail travel was insufficient to sustain early railroad companies in any North American region.

choices.label: E
choices.text: All later-entering railroad companies ultimately outperformed their pioneer counterparts across every financial metric.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that first-mover railroad companies frequently went bankrupt while later entrants remained solvent longer, despite comparable passenger volumes. This supports the hedged conclusion that early entry was, in at least some cases, a financial disadvantage — a direct reading of the pattern with appropriately hedged language.
explanations.A: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus attributes the disadvantage to design inefficiencies and maintenance costs, not management quality. Attributing failure to poor management adds information not in the stimulus.
explanations.C: Too strong: 'sole cause' is an absolute causal claim. The stimulus mentions maintenance costs and design improvements but does not rule out other contributing factors.
explanations.D: Opposite direction: passenger volumes were 'comparable' for early and late lines in their first decades, suggesting demand was not insufficient. This choice contradicts the stimulus.
explanations.E: Too strong and scope creep: 'all later-entering companies' and 'every financial metric' are absolute claims; the stimulus describes general tendencies, not universal outcomes.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves linguistic data with a two-group comparison and a qualifier about context. The correct answer requires integrating both the comparison and the qualifier without dropping either. Traps include answers that drop the contextual qualifier or generalize the finding to all languages.
stimulus: A study of bilingual speakers who acquired both languages before age seven found that when asked to name objects in their weaker language, these speakers produced the correct word significantly faster when the object was presented in a familiar indoor context than when the same object appeared in an unfamiliar outdoor setting. By contrast, when naming objects in their dominant language, response times did not differ between familiar and unfamiliar contexts. The researchers noted that both languages showed comparable accuracy rates regardless of context.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bilingual speakers are always slower to name objects in their weaker language than in their dominant language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For bilingual speakers, contextual familiarity appears to affect word retrieval speed in a weaker language but not in a dominant language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Contextual familiarity improves accuracy as well as speed in object-naming tasks for bilingual speakers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Children who acquire two languages simultaneously before age seven will never experience retrieval difficulties in either language.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The effect of context on language processing is uniform across all bilingual populations regardless of acquisition age.

explanations.correct: The study directly shows that context affected naming speed in the weaker language (faster in familiar contexts) but not in the dominant language (no difference across contexts). The word 'appears' appropriately hedges the causal claim, making this a strong but not absolute inference from the data.
explanations.A: Too strong: 'always slower' is an absolute claim. The study reports response times in specific conditions; it does not establish that the weaker language is always slower across all possible conditions.
explanations.C: Opposite direction / unsupported: the stimulus explicitly states that accuracy rates were comparable regardless of context; context did not improve accuracy.
explanations.D: Too strong and unsupported: 'never experience retrieval difficulties' is an absolute claim not supported by the study, which describes response time differences, not the elimination of all retrieval difficulties.
explanations.E: Scope creep: the study examined early bilinguals (before age seven); generalizing to 'all bilingual populations regardless of acquisition age' goes beyond the data.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents an ethics/law tension in which a legal standard and a common moral intuition diverge across cases, requiring students to identify the inference about the relationship between the two standards rather than affirming either as correct. Traps include answers that endorse one standard as definitively superior or conflate the descriptive and normative claims.
stimulus: Courts in several jurisdictions have held that a person has no legal duty to rescue a stranger in peril, even when rescue would pose no risk to the rescuer. Surveys conducted in those same jurisdictions find that roughly 85 percent of residents believe a bystander who fails to attempt a low-risk rescue of a drowning stranger has acted immorally. Legal scholars who have examined these surveys note that the jurisdictions with no-duty-to-rescue rules have not experienced measurable increases in bystander rescues following the rare enactment of legal duties to rescue in neighboring jurisdictions.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In at least some jurisdictions, the legal standard for rescue duty does not reflect the moral views of the majority of residents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Legal duties to rescue should be enacted in all jurisdictions because most residents believe rescue failures are immoral.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People are more likely to attempt a rescue when there is a legal duty to do so than when there is no such duty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moral intuitions about rescue are unreliable guides to the formulation of legal standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Legal scholars unanimously agree that no-duty-to-rescue rules should be abolished.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly establishes that in jurisdictions with no legal duty to rescue, approximately 85 percent of residents believe failing to attempt a low-risk rescue is immoral. This creates a documented gap between the legal rule (no duty) and the moral view of the majority — a gap that, in at least those jurisdictions, is straightforwardly supported by the data.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported normative claim: the stimulus is purely descriptive. Drawing a prescriptive conclusion ('should be enacted') about what law ought to be goes beyond what the facts support.
explanations.C: Opposite direction: the stimulus states that enacting legal duties to rescue in some jurisdictions did NOT produce measurable increases in bystander rescues in neighboring no-duty jurisdictions — suggesting legal duty does not reliably increase rescue attempts.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus notes a discrepancy between law and moral intuition but does not evaluate moral intuitions as unreliable guides. This is an interpretive judgment not derivable from the facts given.
explanations.E: Too strong and unsupported: the stimulus cites legal scholars' observations about survey data and behavioral effects, but does not describe any scholarly consensus in favor of abolishing the rule.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves arts/economics data with a counterintuitive finding: critical acclaim and commercial performance diverge by genre in a specific streaming context. The correct answer must track the divergence precisely. Traps include an answer that conflates critical and commercial success and one that generalizes beyond the streaming context.
stimulus: An analysis of streaming platform data covering a five-year period found that documentary films receiving major festival awards averaged roughly 40 percent fewer total streams than non-award-winning documentaries released in the same calendar year. Among narrative fiction films, however, festival awards were positively associated with streaming volume: award-winning narrative films averaged approximately 25 percent more streams than non-award-winning narrative films released the same year. Platform analysts noted that award-winning documentaries were predominantly acquired by niche subscription services, while award-winning narrative films were acquired predominantly by large general-audience platforms.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Festival awards reliably increase the commercial streaming success of all film genres.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Niche subscription services offer lower-quality content than large general-audience platforms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For at least one film genre, festival recognition was associated with lower streaming volume rather than higher streaming volume.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Documentary filmmakers should avoid submitting their films to major festivals if they wish to maximize streaming audiences.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The relationship between critical acclaim and streaming performance is identical across documentary and narrative fiction genres.

explanations.correct: The stimulus directly states that award-winning documentaries averaged roughly 40 percent fewer streams than non-award-winning documentaries — a clear case of festival recognition correlating with lower, not higher, streaming volume for that genre. 'At least one genre' hedges appropriately, and the inference is a direct reading of the data.
explanations.A: Too strong and opposite direction: the stimulus shows festival awards were associated with fewer streams for documentaries, directly contradicting the claim that awards 'reliably increase' streaming success 'for all genres.'
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus notes where award-winning films were acquired but makes no claim about the quality of content on different platform types.
explanations.D: Plausible but normative and unsupported: the stimulus reports a correlation; inferring a prescriptive recommendation for filmmakers adds a practical judgment not warranted by the data alone.
explanations.E: Opposite direction: the stimulus explicitly contrasts the two genres, showing the relationship runs in opposite directions — awards are negatively associated with documentary streams but positively associated with narrative fiction streams.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves technology/environmental science data with a multi-variable tension: a renewable energy technology reduces one type of environmental harm while increasing another. The correct inference must acknowledge both dimensions without dismissing either. Traps include answers that credit only one dimension or that make absolute net-benefit or net-harm claims.
stimulus: A lifecycle assessment of utility-scale solar panel installations found that over a 30-year operational period, such installations produce approximately 95 percent less carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour generated than coal-fired plants of equivalent capacity. The same assessment found, however, that manufacturing the panels required substantial quantities of cadmium, a toxic heavy metal, and that disposal of decommissioned panels at the end of their operational life poses documented risks of cadmium leaching into soil and groundwater at landfill sites. The assessment did not evaluate the relative toxicity risk of coal plant emissions to groundwater.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Utility-scale solar installations are environmentally superior to coal-fired plants in every measurable respect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The environmental costs of cadmium disposal from solar panels outweigh the carbon reduction benefits over a 30-year period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Solar panel installations present at least one environmental benefit and at least one environmental risk not shared by their carbon reduction advantage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coal-fired plants pose no significant risk of heavy metal contamination to soil or groundwater.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulators should prohibit the construction of new utility-scale solar installations until cadmium disposal methods are improved.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes both a clear environmental benefit (95% less CO₂ per kWh) and a distinct environmental risk (cadmium leaching at disposal). The correct answer acknowledges both dimensions precisely — 'at least one benefit and at least one risk not shared by their carbon reduction advantage' — without requiring a net judgment the data cannot support.
explanations.A: Too strong: the stimulus explicitly identifies a risk (cadmium contamination) associated with solar panels that is not present in the operational phase of coal plants, so solar is not superior 'in every measurable respect.'
explanations.B: Unsupported and opposite direction: the assessment did not quantify or compare the magnitude of cadmium risk against carbon benefits; making a net-cost-versus-benefit claim goes well beyond the data.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the assessment explicitly states it did not evaluate the relative toxicity risk of coal plant emissions to groundwater, so no conclusion about coal's groundwater risk can be drawn.
explanations.E: Normative and unsupported: the stimulus presents data, not a policy recommendation. Drawing a prescriptive regulatory conclusion requires value judgments the stimulus does not supply.

difficultyReason: The stimulus involves historical/economic data about price controls with a finding that contradicts the standard economic prediction in a specific market subtype. The correct answer must be scoped to that subtype and hedged. Traps include answers that generalize to all price controls, invert the direction, or assign causation without support.
stimulus: Economic historians examining rent control policies in four major European cities between 1920 and 1960 found that in cities where rent controls applied exclusively to housing units occupied before 1925, overall housing construction rates in those cities were not significantly lower than in comparable cities without any rent controls during the same period. Controlled units, however, experienced substantially less maintenance investment than uncontrolled units in the same cities. Additionally, the ratio of controlled to total housing units declined steadily over time as new construction added uncontrolled stock.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rent controls, when applied only to existing housing stock rather than new construction, may not depress overall housing construction rates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rent controls universally reduce maintenance investment in all types of rental housing markets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: European cities that enacted rent controls during this period had higher living standards than those that did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The economic historians concluded that rent control policies were net beneficial to urban residents in the cities studied.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The ratio of controlled to total housing units increased over time as landlords converted uncontrolled units into controlled ones.

explanations.correct: The stimulus shows that rent controls applied only to pre-1925 units did not significantly depress overall housing construction — which runs counter to the standard economic prediction that controls reduce construction. The inference is hedged with 'may not' and correctly scoped to the specific policy design (existing stock only, not new construction), making it a direct and appropriately cautious reading of the data.
explanations.B: Too strong and scope creep: the stimulus shows reduced maintenance in controlled units in these specific cities under this specific policy; 'universally' and 'all types of rental housing markets' vastly overgeneralizes.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported: the stimulus addresses construction rates and maintenance, not living standards. No comparison of living standards is made.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported: the historians described the data; no net-beneficial conclusion is attributed to them by the stimulus.
explanations.E: Opposite direction: the stimulus states the ratio of controlled to total housing declined over time as new (uncontrolled) construction added stock — directly contradicting this answer.
